title: Dividend Yield Explained: How to Calculate and Read It
summary: Dividend yield explained in plain terms: how to calculate it, why it rises when the share price falls, how it differs from total return, and what to check behind a high yield.
body_markdown:
Yield measures one part of what you get from a stock. FINRA's performance guide calls total return generally the most accurate measure of return: the change in value, up or down, plus all the income you collected. Its own example is $2,000 invested at $20 a share, a rise to $25, and $120 in dividends over three years, which is $620, or 31%, before annualizing.


The same arithmetic shows how a yield can look fine while the investment loses money. Using the hypothetical stock above: you buy at $50, collect $2.00 in dividends over the year, and the price ends the year at $45. The yield when you bought was 4%. The total return is ($45 − $50 + $2.00) ÷ $50 = −6%.


A low or zero yield is not a flaw either. Investor.gov's[stocks FAQ](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/stocks) says growth stocks rarely pay dividends and investors buy them hoping for capital appreciation, while income stocks pay dividends consistently. Yield tells you which kind of return a company is sending back to shareholders, not how well the stock will do.


In a taxable account, dividends are also taxable income. IRS[Publication 550](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p550) explains that ordinary dividends are reported on Form 1099-DIV and that some qualify for lower capital-gain rates. FINRA's guide recommends considering taxes when you work out returns. For your own situation, that is a question for a tax professional.
